entries.title: 6 killed, 25 hurt in Labor Day weekend gun violence
entries.summary: <p>More than two dozen people have been shot in Chicago so far over the Labor Day holiday weekend.</p><p>Of the 31 people shot since 5 p.m. Friday, six have died from their injuries, according to Chicago police. At least four teenagers were wounded in separate shootings.</p><p>As of Monday afternoon, the weekend's violence was lower than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/09/02/labor-day-weekend-violence-crime-brandon-johnson-donald-trump" target="_blank" >last Labor Day weekend</a>, when nine people were killed and 52 wounded. The holiday weekend count began Friday at 5 p.m. and continues through 5 a.m. Tuesday. </p><p>Labor Day marks the end of summer. And this season has been historically peaceful in Chicago, compared to past years.</p><p>The city had 122 murders in June, July and August — the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/02/chicago-violence-mayor-johnson-giannoulias-quigley-mendoza" target="_blank" >lowest summer total since 1965</a>. Last year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/01/chicago-crime-murder-homicide-shooting-president-trump-mayor-johnson" target="_blank" >total violence also hit record lows</a> for the first time in decades.</p><p>Despite decreasing violence, six people have been killed and 25 wounded this weekend in shootings mainly on the South and West sides. One person was also injured in a stabbing Friday night. </p><p>The first fatal shooting happened during an argument <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/05/man-fatally-shot-after-argument-in-chicago-lawn" target="_blank" >Friday night in Chicago Lawn</a>. Josh Washington, 28, was fatally shot in his abdomen by a person he was arguing with in the 7300 block of South Kedzie Avenue.</p><p>At around 2 a.m. Saturday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/05/man-fatally-shot-by-2-people-in-west-englewood" target="_blank" >two people fatally shot a man</a> in West Englewood. Enderson Linares, 29, was in the 6500 block of South Laflin Street when the two people shot him and fled in a blue sedan. Linares, who lived on the block where he was killed, was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>A woman was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/06/woman-fatally-shot-near-west-side-home" target="_blank" >found in a Near West Side home</a> suffering from several gunshot wounds just after midnight Sunday. Officers discovered Crystal Salter inside the home in the 2100 block of West Jackson Boulevard. She was pronounced dead at Stroger Hospital. </p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/06/austin-shooting-jerome-kirk" target="_blank" >Springfield man was fatally shot</a> Sunday afternoon in the Austin neighborhood. Jerome Kirk, 20, was sitting in a car in the 300 block of North Lamon Avenue when a person walked up to the vehicle and fired shots.</p><p>A 26-year-old man was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/07/logan-square-shooting" target="_blank" >fatally shot Sunday evening</a> near Kosciuszko Park in the Logan Square neighborhood. Officers found the man, who has not been identified, unresponsive on the ground with a gunshot wound to his back in the 2700 block of North Harding Avenue.</p><p>Around 7:30 a.m. Monday, a 27-year-old woman was found fatally shot in her head inside a Woodlawn home in the 6300 block of South Vernon Avenue. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Police said they were conducting a homicide investigation.</p><p>This summer's two other holiday weekends also saw below-average levels of violence. </p><p>Memorial Day was the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/24/17-people-shot-overnight-chicago" target="_blank" >least deadly weekend</a> for the holiday in 16 years. Two people died and at least 38 were wounded in Chicago.</p><p>Five people were killed and 23 were hurt in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/06/july-fourth-weekend-violence-total-homicides-shootings-injured" target="_blank" >least violent Fourth of July weekend</a> in at least seven years. </p>
entries.author: Kyra Senese

entries.title: 2 boys critically wounded in Grand Boulevard shooting
entries.summary: <p>Two boys, aged 14 and 17, were shot and critically injured Monday afternoon in Grand Boulevard, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers responded to the 4100 block of South Prairie Avenue at about 3:49 p.m. and found the boys suffering from gunshot wounds, police said.</p><p>The 14-year-old boy suffered a gunshot wound to the shoulder and was taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in critical condition, according to police.</p><p>The 17-year-old boy was shot in the head and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center initially in critical condition, police said.</p><p>Area One detectives are investigating the shooting.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Police response blocks Logan Square streets for several hours
entries.summary: <p>A large police presence that included armored vehicles closed streets in Logan Square from late Monday morning into the evening.</p><p>Officers responded to a call for service near the intersection of North Kimball and West Wrightwood Avenues at approximately 11:45 a.m., police said.</p><p>Police did not provide details about the call for service but said the incident was ongoing as of 8 p.m.</p>

entries.title: Girl, 16, shot in Little Village
entries.summary: <p>A 16-year-old girl was injured in a shooting in Little Village Monday evening, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officials said the girl was struck in the back when a man she knew approached her and fired shots.</p><p>The shooting took place in the 2200 block of South Sawyer Avenue at about 7:11 p.m., police said.</p><p>The girl was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital and was initially reported in serious condition, according to police.</p><p>Area Detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: 2 men wounded in West Garfield Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 23-year-old man and a 36-year-old man were wounded in a shooting Monday afternoon in West Garfield Park, Chicago police said.</p><p>The two men were near a sidewalk along the 3800 block of West Adams Street at about 4:28 p.m. when a white two-door vehicle approached them. </p><p>Two men exited the vehicle and fired multiple shots at the victims, police said. </p><p>The alleged assailants then returned to the vehicle and fled south through an alley toward Jackson Boulevard, according to police. </p><p>The 36-year-old man suffered two gunshot wounds to his leg and was taken to Stroger Hospital in unknown condition, police said.</p><p>The 23-year-old man was shot once in the buttocks and was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he was initially listed in good condition, according to police.</p><p>Area Four detectives are investigating.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Bears have had plenty of elite players — just not at quarterback
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> finally have “that guy” in quarterback Caleb Williams.</p><p>At least they think they have that guy.</p><p>Don’t they? </p><p>“From what little I have watched, and just from hearing from people that have seen him week in and week out, what I hear is he doesn’t make the routine play as often as he should make it,” one critic told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Well, there is Williams’ 58.1% completion rate last season to think about. It was down from his rookie number — 62.5% — which wasn’t all the great itself. Sure, one supposes the megatalented 24-year-old could be a bit more accurate.</p><p>“Like a guy wide-open — you don’t miss a guy wide-open,” the critic said.</p><p>But Williams made so many epic throws last season, particularly on broken plays, it’s kind of easy to overlook the plays he didn’t make — and, yeah, there were lots of them — within the regular flow of the offense. Not that big a deal when you’re pulling out the “W” in the end, is it?</p><p>“You gotta make routine plays routine,” the critic said. “It shouldn’t even be a thought. Then you wouldn’t have to do the theatrical parts at the end of the game to try to win. You do the routine [expletive] during the game, and you’re probably sitting on the bench in the fourth quarter — the game’s over.”</p><p>Man, this critic had some opinions.</p><p>Should we out him?</p><p>Fine — it was Jim McMahon, the only Super Bowl-winning Bears quarterback.</p><p>“Look, there’s no knock,” McMahon told the Sun-Times a few weeks after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/01/18/bears-rams-score-2026-nfl-playoffs-results" >Bears lost a 20-17 heartbreaker</a> to the Rams in an NFC divisional playoff game at snowy Soldier Field. “You keep making routine plays with the cast that he has around him — routine plays that are going to get you where you want to go — and then when you have to make the spectacular play, he’s able to do that because of his athleticism.”</p><p>Debating the merits of Williams is a fun thing to do because — we can all agree — he has so many of them. He might have the most physical talent of any quarterback to put on a Bears uniform. He seems to have the determination and confidence required to become great. He certainly has the clutch gene. Add the impacts of offensive-oriented coach Ben Johnson and a front office that’s prioritizing offense like few, if any, Bears teams have before, and it doesn’t take a blue-and-orange-goggled fan to see a potential superstar at arguably the most important position in sports.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/1DgjDi774FI?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Caleb Williams makes MIRACULOUS throw to Cole Kmet to tie it late for Bears | SNF | NFL on NBC"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Then again, what would Chicago know about superstar QBs?</p><h3><b>Here’s to Sid Luckman</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The most prominent Bear of the team’s greatest decade — the 1940s — won four NFL championships, was a five-time first-team All-Pro, led the league in passing yards and touchdowns multiple times and made the Hall of Fame. The Bears’ most accomplished QB ever? Discussion over.</p><p>But since then ... oof. It ain’t pretty, folks. The Bears have an infamous history at the position — maybe the worst of any NFL franchise — and they’ve earned it.</p><p>They had a major celebrity in McMahon, the “Punky QB,” who was drafted in the first round in 1982, won all the marbles in 1985 and finished his time in Chicago with a lopsided win-loss record of 46-15 as a starter. But McMahon had a hard time staying healthy, and even when good to go he was far from prolific. Those Bears had Walter Payton to run the ball, stone-cold killers on defense and a coach, Mike Ditka, who was as at ease with opening up the passing game as he was with singing during the seventh-inning stretch at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Another way to frame McMahon’s performance: In 66 games as a Bear, he threw for 11,203 yards and 67 touchdowns. Decades later, first-round bust Mitch Trubisky would throw for 10,609 yards and 64 touchdowns in only 51 games. McMahon was miles better than Trubisky, no doubt, but there’s also the context of some 70 years of organization futility under center.</p><p>The NFL began tracking quarterback wins as a stat in 1950, too late for Luckman. Since that time, the Bears’ leader in the category is Jay Cutler. That it’s Cutler isn’t entirely surprising given he was their No. 1 guy from 2009 until the injury that ended his 2016 season five games in. But the polarizing Cutler was known for his big arm and his sullen attitude far more than he was for winning — the Bears were 51-51 in his starts — and 51 QB wins is a hilariously puny figure for a franchise leader.</p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-750000" runner who, despite twice leading the NFL in interceptions, still leads the Bears by a long stretch in yards (23,443) and touchdowns (154). But his time with the Bears would be a footnote in most other places.</p><p>Tom Brady had 219 QB wins with the Patriots, who also had Steve Grogan (75) and Drew Bledsoe (63). The Dolphins had Dan Marino (147) and Bob Griese (92). The 49ers had Joe Montana (100), Steve Young (91) and John Brodie (74). The Steelers had Ben Roethlisberger (165) and Terry Bradshaw (107). The Packers had Brett Favre (160), Aaron Rodgers (147) and Bart Starr (94). It goes on and on.</p><p>The Cowboys have five with more QB wins than Cutler had here: Troy Aikman (94), Roger Staubach (85), Dak Prescott (83 and counting), Tony Romo (78) and Danny White (62). Even the division rival Lions and Vikings have richer histories than the Bears at the position. Detroit has seen Matthew Stafford (74) and Bobby Layne (53), and current starter Jared Goff (48) should blow by Cutler’s mark this season. Minneapolis can boast at least a little of having Fran Tarkenton (91) and Tommy Kramer (54).</p><p>Perhaps Williams will play and thrive here long enough to hit triple digits in QB wins someday. That’s the dream. If he gets there, he’ll likely surpass 4,000 passing yards in a season multiple times along the way. As it stands, though, the Bears are the only NFL team yet to have a 4,000-yard passer since the league moved to a 16-game schedule in 1978. Williams got to 3,942 last season, eclipsing Erik Kramer’s 30-year-old Bears record of 3,838.</p><p>“I’m proud that it stood up for that long,” Kramer told the Sun-Times. “Joe Montana didn’t have a 4,000-yard season. Roger Staubach didn’t. Terry Bradshaw didn’t. Why that became the standard, I don’t know.”</p><p>Of the nine quarterbacks the Bears have made first-round draft picks — starting with Luckman in 1939 — five came in between McMahon and Williams. Jim Harbaugh, pick No. 26 in 1987, had a QB record of 35-30 as a Bear. Cade McNown, the 12th pick in 1999, was a 3-12 all-time bust. Rex Grossman, taken 22nd in 2003, went 19-12 — a million thank-yous, 2006 defense — and got all the way to a Super Bowl. Justin Fields, No. 11 in 2021, left with a record of 10-28.</p><p>It’s almost amazing, in hindsight, to remember all the public debate about whether the Bears should stick with Fields or trade him and draft Williams. Such folly, indeed.</p><h3>Williams is better than three Grossmans</h3><h3></h3><p>Not to pick on anyone, but imagine how current coach Johnson would flip out over Grossman’s 54.6% completion rate (28th in the league), 73.9 rating (24th), 20 interceptions and eight fumbles in 2006. But, hey, those Bears were 13-3 and nearly went all the way. So what if it ended up being Grossman’s only full season as QB1 out of his six in Chicago?</p><p>“I had a lot of ups, a lot of downs, some injuries, went to the Super Bowl, got benched, came back,” Grossman said on a Barstool podcast this year. “I made a ton of money; I had so much fun; I played in the Super Bowl. Everybody can say whatever the [expletive] you want to say, I still had the best six years of my life. You would do it if you could do it. I loved it.”</p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-800000" name="image-800000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e414e40/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3033x1702+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2Fbc%2Fb40802c649d3b1afc5d61be6dcaf%2Fgrosssman.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/40e8e96/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3033x1702+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2Fbc%2Fb40802c649d3b1afc5d61be6dcaf%2Fgrosssman.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1566b89/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3033x1702+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F04%2Fbc%2Fb40802c649d3b1afc5d61be6dcaf%2Fgrosssman.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Bears quarterback Rex Grossman leads his team onto the field before their game against the Green Bay Packers on Sept. 10, 2006, at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin. There is no better comparison than the one with the bleepin’ Packers.</p><p>In the third game of 1992, the Packers’ then-starter, Don Majkowski, got hurt. Enter Brett Favre, who would start 13 times that year and every game to come until the 2007 season was over. From then through 2022, it would be all Aaron Rodgers except for the scattered occasions when a total of four other Packers were forced into starting duty. That’s a 31-season run with two stars and a handful of meaningless cameos.</p><p>The Bears, on the other hand, started 19 quarterbacks just from 1992 to 2008, preceding Cutler’s arrival. From Cutler’s time through 2022, there were 16 more. Thirty-five starters in 31 years is beyond absurd. It’s stultifying and tragic.</p><p>Ah, our Bears. What strange history.</p><p>A curious enough, strange enough person could sift through an all-time list of Bears quarterbacks, pick a few at random and discover God only knows what. That’s the plan right now, anyway. Here goes.</p><p><b>Milton Romney (1926-28):</b> You know you’re already asking, and the answer is Mitt Romney’s father’s cousin. Suffice it to say, the Miltster isn’t enshrined in Canton, Ohio.</p><p><b>Bernie Masterson (1934-40):</b> Let’s just say he never quite mastered the forward pass.</p><p><b>Johnny Lujack (1948-51):</b> The Heisman Trophy winner from Notre Dame played defensive back and had eight interceptions as a rookie. A year later, he led the NFL in all major passing categories. He started two more seasons after that, with Luckman — and George Blanda — behind him. Not bad.</p><p></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-030000" name="image-030000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4433a0a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2270x1274+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc4%2Fd0%2Fb101f0054ab88cee3d673f04efa2%2Fconcannon.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3bb56ef/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2270x1274+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc4%2Fd0%2Fb101f0054ab88cee3d673f04efa2%2Fconcannon.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4ca874d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2270x1274+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc4%2Fd0%2Fb101f0054ab88cee3d673f04efa2%2Fconcannon.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Bears quarterback Jack Concannon speaks to head coach George Halas. entries.title: Cop responding to call of service hurt in Near West Side crash
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago police officer responding to a call of service was injured in a crash Monday night on the Near West Side. </p><p>The officer, who was in a marked vehicle with emergency lights activated, was struck by a silver sedan that field to yield at an intersection in the 500 block of South Ashland Avenue around 10:25 p.m., police said. </p><p>The officer suffered a cut to his forehead and was taken to an area hospital in good condition, officials said. The driver of the sedan, a 26-year-old man, suffered a knee injury and was taken to Stroger Hospital in good condition. </p><p>Two other passengers in the sedan declined medical attention, police said. </p><p>A citation was issued to the sedan driver. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man seriously injured, woman missing after vehicle plunges into Little Calumet River in West Pullman
entries.summary: <p>A man was seriously injured and a woman was missing after a vehicle drove into the Little Calumet River early Tuesday in West Pullman on the Far South Side. </p><p>The vehicle, which was occupied by five adults, was in the 13000 block of South Indiana Avenue around 2:30 a.m. when it lost control, struck a barrier and fell into the water, Chicago police said. </p><p>One man was rescued by the marine unit and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center in serious condition, police said. </p><p>A woman was missing and a search for her continued, officials said. </p><p>Three others were able to make it to land safely and were treated by Chicago Fire Department officials, police said. </p><p>The Major Accidents Investigation Unit were investigating.<br></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Dear Abby: Would rather not keep in touch with talkative old friend
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Two years ago, I ran into an old friend I hadn't seen in more than 25 years. We went to dinner the following week. The dinner lasted three hours. Abby, she talked the entire time! It was a mix of grandiose stories, complaints about her health, complaints about her relationships and an attempt to make me feel guilty for not contacting her sooner. I tried to excuse it, telling myself, "It's been decades; of course she has a lot to say."</p><p>Every subsequent interaction followed the same pattern, with an expectation of far more of my time and energy than I was comfortable giving. At one point, she even sprinkled in a little condescension about my political leaning. I started feeling anxious before seeing her and drained afterward.</p><p>Over a year ago, I decided to take a step back. I told her I'd reach out when I felt up to socializing again, and I haven't contacted her since. Despite that, she's continued to call and text. I don't want to hurt her feelings, but I have no interest in the friendship. At the same time, continuing to ignore her feels unkind. I know this will hurt her, but what's the most honest (and least painful) way to tell her I don't want further contact? — <i>GHOSTING HER ISN'T WORKING</i></p><p><b>DEAR GHOSTING:</b> Unless you want to fully commit to the ghosting strategy by blocking this woman's number, stop avoiding her calls and texts. Decline her next invitation by telling her you are trying to focus on other parts of your life right now. That's the truth. If she persists, tell her getting together isn't feasible right now and you prefer that she let you initiate contact in the future. If she still doesn't get the message, blocking her is your only option.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a young neighbor who is interested in social causes. She advocates stopping animal abuse, has run the race against breast cancer and volunteers to feed the homeless. I enjoy talking to her because she's so passionate about these causes.</p><p>She has told me she feels alienated from her schoolmates, who don't like her "constant preaching." Even her mother has told her she should "slow down and enjoy being a teenager." The girl has told me I'm the only one who understands her. This is uncomfortable because she should be able to confide in her mother. Her mom should be proud of her for not engaging in the harmful behavior some teens do. The girl is lonely at school, and I don't know what to tell her. Have you any ideas? — <i>SUPPORTIVE NEIGHBOR IN OHIO</i></p><p><b>DEAR SUPPORTIVE NEIGHBOR:</b> Feeling some sense of alienation is part of being a teenager. I don't think the girl's mother suggesting she slow down and enjoy being a teen is a criticism, and you shouldn't assume that the woman isn't proud of her daughter.</p><p>Sometimes people — not just teenagers — need someone in their lives who is willing to listen and offer praise. Because the girl relates well to you, continue to fill that role. However, if her "constant preaching" is alienating her schoolmates, it couldn't hurt to suggest that no one ever learned anything by talking — she should also do some listening. It's good advice, and it applies to situations other than high school.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: 2 men shot to death in Englewood home; 1 in custody
entries.summary: <p>Charges are pending for a suspect in custody after two men were shot to death during an argument at an Englewood home late Monday on the South Side. </p><p>Around 11:55 p.m., the two men were arguing with someone they knew inside the home in the 600 block of West 74th Street when they were shot, Chicago police said. </p><p>One of the men, 45, was shot in the chest and neck while the other, 32, was shot in the chest, police said. Both were pronounced dead at the scene. </p><p>A man was arrested at the scene and two firearms were recovered, officials said. </p><p>Charges were pending. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Photos: What Operation Midway Blitz left behind
entries.summary: <p>One year ago today, President Donald Trump's administration sent hundreds of immigration agents into Chicago area communities with the stated goal of arresting and deporting immigrants who they accused of committing crimes.</p><p>The surge at times felt like a siege. The deportation campaign was one that residents could see, hear and feel.</p><p>Helicopters hovered overhead for hours. Unmarked SUVs — sometimes without license plates — patrolled the streets, full of agents in military-style clothes. Neighbors' whistles and family members' screams became an unwanted daily soundtrack.</p><p>While the signs of the chaos dissipated once Operation Midway Blitz winded down, remnants are still visible entries.title: A look back at how Operation Midway Blitz played out
entries.summary: <p>President Donald Trump vowed at the start of his second term to deport thousands of immigrants he accused of being criminals.</p><p>The Trump administration ramped up immigration enforcement in his first several months in office before launching Operation Midway Blitz in the Chicago area last September. It was a sweeping deportation campaign that brought hundreds of federal immigration agents into the region and upended communities.</p><p>The charge led to the shooting death of an immigrant father, the mobilization of thousands of protesters and growing calls for elected officials to protect residents from federal authorities.</p><p>Chicago and Illinois have seen resulting policy changes, the prosecution of immigrants and federal agents, and continued investigations into alleged prosecutorial misconduct.</p><p>This is a timeline of events on the one-year anniversary of Operation Midway Blitz:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d20000" name="html-embed-module-d20000"></a><script> (function(window, document) { 'use strict'; entries.title: Art Institute unveils ode to ‘relentless experimenter’ Mary Cassatt, including tale of long lost Chicago mural
entries.summary: <p>In its newly unveiled ode to painter <a class="Link" href="https://www.artic.edu/exhibitions/10487/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism" target="_blank" ><u>Mary Cassatt</u></a>, The Art Institute of Chicago pays tribute to a woman who lived on her own terms.</p><p>The new exhibit “<a class="Link" href="https://www.artic.edu/exhibitions/10487/mary-cassatt-after-impressionism" target="_blank" ><u>Mary Cassatt: After Impressionism</u>”</a>— the museum’s marquee show of the fall season and its first deep-dive into Cassatt in more than 25 years — features about 70 of Cassatt’s paintings, pastels and prints. The show includes “The Child’s Bath,” a standout part of the museum’s permanent collection since it was acquired in 1910.</p><p>Cassatt was born in 1844 in Pennsylvania but lived most of her life in France. She is perhaps best known for her association with the French Impressionists, including Edgar Degas, who invited her to exhibit with the avant-garde clique of art radicals.</p><p>But this new exhibit looks beyond that period of Cassatt’s career to all that came next and reinterprets the groundbreaking American female artist, 100 years after her death.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The show also highlights the artist’s ties to Chicago, including a now-lost mural commissioned for the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The show begins with Cassatt’s early works, some of which demonstrate a Renaissance influence. But there are also signs of what Cassatt became best known for: depicting fellow women as they were in their everyday lives, whether reading the newspaper, seeing an opera or tending to children.</p><p>The exhibition then leads attendees down a hallway to encounter “The Child’s Bath,” which shows a mother in a striped dress with her hair pulled back, washing her youngster’s feet. On Monday, one attendee held her own fussy toddler and pointed to the picture on the wall.</p><p>The instantly recognizable 1893 work is, as Madsen says, “the bridge” to the rest of the exhibit. In one direction, the show dives into Cassatt’s exploration of printmaking, inspired by a show she saw in Paris, featuring Japanese woodblock prints from the 17th to 19th centuries.</p><p>“She was really energized by what she saw,” said Madsen. “And was thinking about how she could translate those aesthetics into something that worked for her.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Michigan Ave.<br><b>Info:</b> A $7 exhibition ticket is required in addition to general admission, except for museum members</div> </div><p>The other side of the gallery showcases Cassatt’s ongoing depiction of mothers and children. Despite Cassatt not having children of her own, Madsen said she brought a “seriousness” and “a sense of purpose” to her subjects.</p><p>“There's a real sense of presence there that is a note that she hits on again and again,” Madsen said, adding that Cassatt is also in an ongoing exploration of her technical expertise, through color, material and pattern.</p><p>“That's one of the things that, for me, is so fascinating about Cassatt that it's always about this subject, but it's always also about what she can do formally with the materials in hand,” Madsen said.</p><div class="Enhancement" From Hubert Howe Bancroft, “The Book of the Fair” (Bancroft, 1893), 3:269. Courtesy of the Art Institute.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The massive piece helped raise Cassatt’s profile in the United States and made her one of the early women artists to complete a public mural in the U.S. And, due to Cassatt’s assertiveness, she also earned the same pay as the male muralists in the fair, according to Madsen.</p><p>The Woman’s Building was demolished after the fair. And Cassatt’s mural was either lost or destroyed — it was last accounted for in 1912. Still, Madsen said, it’s an important part of the story. “One of the objectives of the exhibition is to piece together that story and try to bring it back to life for visitors,” Madsen said.</p><p>The exhibit does that, in part, through a series of easel-sized artworks, which feature many of the same women and similar scenes that were depicted in the mural.</p><p>Through her three-year exploration of Cassatt, Madsen said she gained a better understanding of the artist as a “relentless experimenter.”</p><p>“She is pathbreaking at every moment, really,” said Madsen. “I think the determination, the grit to go out and do something that is not what's expected of you, but is what you want for yourself, is a story that many of us can cheer for and take something from.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: A Chicago couple was poised to open a new Lincoln Avenue bistro. Then the city shut down their street
entries.summary: <p>On a recent August morning, Mary Nedbalski, co-owner of the forthcoming <a class="Link" href="https://gunnyspub.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Gunny’s Pub</u></a> on Lincoln Avenue, went to work, only to discover that the city had shut down the street outside.</p><p>The surprise street shutdown could last until October — poor timing for a bar and bistro set to open Sept. 16.</p><p>This wasn’t the first setback that Nedbalski and her husband, Marty O’Connor, faced in opening their new Lincoln Park neighborhood bar and restaurant. Approximately two months earlier, the city began replacing the sewer line along a three-block stretch of Lincoln Avenue starting at Racine Avenue and Diversey Parkway.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Business owners were told the work would be finished in July, O’Connor said. But the severe storms that hit the city on Fourth of July weekend caused a giant sinkhole, and the pipes beneath Gunny’s filled with gravel and debris.</p><p>Now, Gunny’s is in an uneasy position for a new restaurant, with an opening date and full menu of classic and craft cocktails and Midwestern supper club staples.</p><p>With the street closure complicating the opening, Nedbalski and O’Connor have taken to social media to humorously explain their plight. They’re hoping that neighbors will walk or bike over to their establishment at 2642 N. Lincoln Ave.</p><p>“The City of Chicago decided to give us a massive twist," O'Connor said in an Instagram <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DchkaxsNJ7H/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>video</u></a>. “Just because the city shut down the road doesn’t mean we can’t open.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="InstagramUrl"> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Nedbalski said notice of the nearly two-month street closure came late for Gunny’s and other businesses on Lincoln Avenue.</p><p>“It sounds like no one was really kept in the loop with the city, including the alderman’s office,” she said. “But I mean, even a heads-up of, ‘Hey, we’ve had a problem’ … You could go up and down the street with a printed piece of paper to let us know beforehand. Any level of, ‘Hey, by the way, we’re cutting off your entire customer base for three whole city blocks.’”</p><p>Nedbalski used <a class="Link" href="http://pacer.ai" target="_blank" ><u>Pacer.ai</u></a> to analyze foot traffic on their street and found it’s steadily declining. “We’re down more than 5,000 to 6,000 visits a week, and it’s only getting worse. So the only thing we can do is support the businesses around us and open anyway,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure previously home to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.eater.com/2019/3/25/18280741/racine-plumbing-lincoln-park-sports-bar-closing-april-publican-anker-closed-new-kahan-restaurant" target="_blank" ><u>Racine Plumbing Bar & Grill</u></a>.</p><p>What sold them on the location was the massive skylight in the rear of the restaurant. And when O’Connor saw the back room, he felt that it “yearned” for “a great dinner” service.</p><p>Gunny’s is named after O’Connor’s late dog. “My dog, Gunny, was a pheasant and duck hunting dog. So that kind of helped us inspire the menu for an American bistro with that Midwest hunter-gatherer flair,” he said.</p><p>The couple originally brought in chef Mike McKinnell for some consulting work. They ultimately offered him the job as head chef.</p><p>With McKinnell’s help, they’re hoping to add other types of upland game, beyond duck, to the seasonal menu. That might include quail or venison, and in the spring, rabbit.</p><p>Gunny’s will focus on “bar-esque” foods and shareables in the front, but in the back, the focus is on casual fine dining, McKinnell said.</p><p>McKinnell has worked in notable kitchens across Chicago and New York City. In Manhattan, he sharpened his skills at Oceana and Root & Bone. In Chicago, he ended up at the now-closed Dusek's Board & Beer at Thalia Hall, and later at Mordecai with Matthias Merges, where he met O’Connor, who was bartending and serving.</p><p>“Somewhere on that high-end, but the lowest level of the high-end, is really what I’d love to see for [Gunny’s],” McKinnell said. He wants diners to feel like they’re stepping into a proper bistro grounded in classic cooking techniques, but infused with unmistakable Chicago panache.</p><p>Among the large plates on the menu at Gunny’s are the <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DcwKuruAZof/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>bavette steak</u></a>, served with salsa verde and wedge-cut fries and the Gunny’s take on a Chicago classic: Italian beef with a house-made giardiniera. There’s a smashburger, too, served with griddled onion, shaved pickles, American cheese and bacon mayonnaise sauce.</p><p>As far as shareables, one of Gunny’s specialties is the poutine, which includes duck confit. See also: stuffed cheese bread, a pull-apart made with a sourdough boule. Its crevices are stuffed with gooey Hook’s yellow and Laubscher white cheddar cheese, herbs, and crispy, chicharrón-style duck cracklings.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: In new cookbook ‘Kari,’ curry gets its due, with a Midwestern accent
entries.summary: <p>Sheil Shukla keeps a lot on his proverbial plate. The internal medicine physician, husband, father of three and creative wrangler of showstopping, vegan South Asian dishes published his second cookbook, “<a class="Link" href="https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/771370/kari-by-sheil-shukla/" target="_blank" ><u>Kari: Reimagined Plant-Based Indian Recipes</u></a>,” on Aug. 18. ($35, DK [Penguin Random House]). </p><p>The followup to 2022’s “Plant-Based India,” “Kari” and its 75 plant-based recipes lean more personal, drawing on the author’s lived experiences as the son of Gujarati immigrant parents who was raised in the Milwaukee suburbs and formed his culinary viewpoint in Chicago. Named for and centered on curry, it offers up aromatic, make-ahead sauces and simple accompaniments that can work into folks’ weekly cooking repertoire with a little planning.</p><p>“‘Kari’ is a melding of the Indian recipes I know, the Thai and Japanese and Vietnamese recipes I love — taking a little from different experiences I’ve had around the country, experiencing the true melting pot we have and should continue to have in the U.S. — tailored to the home kitchen,” Shukla said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sheil Shukla</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Growing up, Shukla’s eating life was anchored in the homestyle western coastal Indian cooking prepared by his mother and grandmother, like simmered daal with rice, seasonal shaak (vegetables) and rotli (thin wheat flatbreads). The family traveled and dined out often — inspired by Asian food especially, from rich, creamy North Indian and Punjabi to sweet, sour, fiery Thai. Shukla and his brother relished the rarer Americanized indulgences, like chicken tenders and Olive Garden fettuccine Alfredo.</p><p>Shukla moved to Chicago for undergrad in 2011 and studied molecular biology and graphic design, keen to pursue creative arts as he worked toward a career in medicine. He’s now a practicing physician in Glenview and Vernon Hills, while he and wife Rachel raise a toddler and two young twins. A vegan since 2015, Shukla, 33, has documented his plant-based cooking journey on Instagram, where he’s known as <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/plantbasedartist/" target="_blank" ><u>@plantbasedartist</u></a>, culminating in “Plant-Based India,” which showcases the beauty and health benefits of properly zhuzhed plants.</p><p>Now, he turns his attention to curry (or gravy as it’s sometimes denoted throughout “Kari”). Derived from the Tamil word “kari,” it describes a wide-ranging set of aromatic dishes from numerous Asian cultures. Over the centuries, colonizers erased the regional nuance from the term, instead lumping all spiced gravies and stews under the umbrella term “curry.” In the book, Shukla defines kari as a dish consisting of an “aromatic sauce with vegetables and/or proteins, attributed to South Asian and East Asian traditions” — be it sweet, sour and umami-rich Thai gaeng; mellow, savory Japanese kare; or citrusy, lemongrass-scented Vietnamese ca ri.</p><p>“The curries in the book explore that overlap and my own sort of creativity in creating dishes that aren't part of one cuisine, but part of every one at the same time,” Shukla said. Importantly, he added, they don’t overpower the produce, pushing back on the “common criticism of Indian cuisine that it’s too heavily spiced.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div influences. Tangy, creamy cashew- and tomato-based makhani sauce scented with cumin and fennel stands in for rich, savory Japanese-style curry and crunchy battered tofu for the traditional tonkatsu (pork cutlet).</p><p>In case you’re wondering, Shukla and his wife don’t whip up dozen-ingredient gravies on any old Tuesday. Instead, they like to prepare foundational simmer sauces on the weekends to form “flavor bases” that they can pull from the fridge or freezer during the week to build simple weeknight meals. The book includes a handy matrix of sauces (Tikka Masala, Beet Korma, Makhani Sauce, Lemongrass Yellow Curry) and numerous lower-lift applications for them (nachos, crispy potatoes, noodle soup, bread pizza). Elsewhere, multicultural chutneys, dressings and glazes shine up pan-fried tofu with broccoli and dress endive and apple salad, pasta or rice.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatLeft> <div A Midwest farmers market vegetable index in the back of the book groups recipes by ingredients commonly found at Chicago-area markets throughout the year.</p><p>As we reach the last gasps of Midwestern summer, many of us are staring down a veritable crush of corn and summer squashes. But don’t fear the gourd. Shukla offers up crisp, golden zucchini and corn pakoras, the beloved, versatile Indian snacks made by dabbing presalted vegetables in spiced besan (chickpea flour), frying them till crunchy. They’re served alongside a bold chutney — in this case, sweet, <b>warmly spiced</b> mango, with unexpected depth and roundness from a blob of miso.</p><p>“If you find yourself wondering what to do with that haul of farmers market veggies or an unfamiliar squash, making pakoras is generally a good move,” Shukla said. “These fritters are a joyous celebration of summer. class="Figure-credit"><p>Sheil Shukla</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Zucchini Corn Pakoras with Mango Miso Masala Chutney</h3><p>Serves 4 as an appetizer or snack</p><p>Tempting though it may be, don’t skip presalting the vegetables, Sheil Shukla <b>said</b>. “This draws out the moisture from the veg that then, when combined with the chickpea flour, becomes the batter that keeps everything together.”</p><p><b>Ingredients</b><br>1 large zucchini, cut into thin matchsticks (about 3 cups/300 g)<br>1 small red onion, thinly sliced (about 1 cup/150 g)<br>1 cup (125 g) fresh or frozen corn kernels<br>2 to 3 scallions, thinly sliced<br>Salt<br>2 garlic cloves, minced (about 2 teaspoons)<br>2 teaspoons minced ginger<br>½ teaspoon cumin seeds<br>¼ teaspoon ajwain (carom) seeds, optional (see Note 1)<br>Freshly cracked black pepper, to taste<br>½ cup (60 g) besan or chickpea flour, plus more as needed<br>Neutral oil, for frying</p><p><b>For serving</b><br>Chaat masala or salt, optional<br>Chopped fresh cilantro leaves, optional<br>½ cup (120 ml) Mango Miso Masala Chutney (recipe follows)</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Combine the zucchini, onions, corn, and scallions and 3⁄4 teaspoon salt in a large bowl, massaging the salt evenly into the vegetables with clean hands. Set aside for about 10 minutes, squeezing the vegetables every few minutes, until the vegetables release liquid and feel wet; you may see about 1 tablespoon liquid accumulating at the bottom of the bowl.</p><p>Stir in the garlic, ginger, cumin seeds, ajwain seeds (if using), and black pepper. Incorporate the besan with clean <b>fingers</b>, 1 tablespoon at a time, until the mixture just starts holding together and the vegetables are thinly and evenly coated in the batter. Add a sprinkling of water with your fingers if the mixture is too dry.</p><p>Place a cooling rack on top of a paper towel-lined baking sheet (for easier cleanup).</p><p>Heat about ½ inch (1 cm) oil to 350°F (180°C) in a large skillet over medium heat. You’ll know the oil is ready when you place a small amount of the pakora batter into the oil and it sizzles immediately.</p><p>Working in batches, place small heaps (2 to 3 tablespoons each) of the pakora mixture in the skillet, 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5 cm) apart, and flatten slightly. Cook until the pakoras start to brown on the bottom, 3 to 4 minutes. Flip and <b>flatten</b> slightly, and cook until browned on the other side, 3 to 4 minutes.</p><p>Transfer to the cooling rack to drain any excess oil. Top with a light sprinkle of chaat masala and cilantro, if using. Serve immediately with the chutney (see Note 2).</p><p><b>Notes</b><br>1. Ajwain seeds, which provide an herbal, thyme-like flavor, are often found in pakoras. It’s worth buying a small quantity to try.<br>2. These pakoras can be made up to 2 hours ahead and reheated in the oven on a parchment paper–lined sheet pan at 400°F (200°C) for about 5 minutes, until crisp and heated through.</p><p><i>Reprinted with permission from “Kari” by Sheil Shukla, copyright © 2026 by Sheil Shukla. entries.title: ‘You want to show the world and bear witness’: Sun-Times, WBEZ reporters on last fall’s deportation campaign
entries.summary: <p>The Department of Homeland Security announced the official launch of Operation Midway Blitz — an aggressive campaign aimed at arresting immigrants and deporting them — on Sept. 8, 2025.</p><p>Last fall, it seemed like the federal government had declared war on the city of Chicago.</p><p>Under the leadership of then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino, federal agents shot and killed an unarmed man, they rammed into cars, pointed guns into protesters' faces and slammed observers to the ground. They grabbed day care workers, tamale vendors and U.S. citizens. And they maximized fear in communities across the Chicago area.</p><p>The government claimed it was going after criminals. “This operation will target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens in Chicago,” DHS said in a news release.</p><p>But a Chicago Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis of<b> </b>data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement found a majority of those held at the ICE processing facility in west suburban Broadview or in other Chicago locations had no criminal conviction<b>.</b></p><p>Immigration enforcement today is quieter and less visible, but the Trump administration is still detaining hundreds of people per month with no criminal records.</p><p>So, how did we get here?</p><p>In the special documentary “Bearing Witness to the Blitz,” WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times journalists Chip Mitchell, Ashlee Rezin, Mariah Woelfel and Adriana Cardona-Maguigad reflect on some of the key moments of Operation Midway Blitz and the lingering effects of the sweeping enforcement operation today.</p><p>Listen wherever you get your podcasts or click the red button up top.</p>

entries.title: Lincoln-Way East students plan walkout over racial harassment incident at Homewood-Flossmoor football game
entries.summary: <p>Lincoln-Way East principal Toriano Griggs addressed a possible student walkout on Wednesday in an email to school families on Tuesday. </p><p>"We are also aware of information circulating about a potential student walkout on Wednesday, September 9," Griggs wrote in the email. "While we will not prevent students from participating in a walkout, we will manage any student walkout or protest in accordance with procedures outlined in the student handbook and with appropriate safety precautions in place. Individuals who are not Lincoln-Way East students or authorized visitors will not be permitted on campus. Our priority will continue to be maintaining a safe and orderly environment for all students and staff."</p><p>Police removed multiple people from the Lincoln-Way East student section in the third quarter of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/04/lincoln-way-east-football-homewood-flossmoor" >Friday’s game</a> between visiting Lincoln-Way East and Homewood-Flossmoor in Flossmoor.</p><p>The teams, most fans and media were unaware of what had happened, but photos and videos began appearing on social media on Saturday morning. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/05/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racial-harassment" >Later on Saturday, both schools addressed the incident.</a></p><p>According to a statement from H-F superintendent Jennifer Norrell and principal Clinton Alexander, “five Lincoln-Way East student fans made a very bad choice to engage in disrespectful and racist harassment towards H-F students seated in the bleachers.”</p><p>Alexander was at the game. The statement goes on to say that H-F is working with Lincoln-Way East and local authorities “as we consider all options to protect against this in the future, including legal options.”</p><p>Griggs addressed the incident on Tuesday with the Lincoln-Way East student body. </p><p>"By now, many of you have seen videos, social media posts, or news reports about the incident," Griggs wrote in the email to families. "I have personally reviewed videos and spoken with students, families, and others who were there.</p><p>"I want to be very clear: the racial slurs, monkey noises, and racist gestures that occurred Friday night were hurtful and completely unacceptable. This behavior has no place at Lincoln-Way East or anywhere else.</p><p>"We reminded students that being a Griffin is about much more than wearing blue and white. It is about how we treat others, having the courage to speak up when something is wrong, and understanding the responsibility that comes with representing our school...Friday night was deeply disappointing. What matters now is how we respond, what we learn, and what we do moving forward. Our actions must demonstrate the values we expect from the Lincoln-Way East community."</p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydvjujl-l-t/" target="_blank" >The toll of Trump’s 68-day Blitz on Chicago</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydvjujl-l-i/" target="_blank" >Lauren FitzPatrick</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydvjujl-l-d/" target="_blank" >Alden Loury</a></h5><p><b>The wounded city</b>: Chicago, long home to immigrants, had never seen federal enforcement like this before. Hundreds of immigration officers streamed into Chicago starting one year ago. They came from across the country, dispatched to execute "Operation Midway Blitz." President Donald Trump had been warning of accelerating his mass deportation campaign in Chicago, targeting cities and states with sanctuary policies protecting immigrants. The surge lasted from Sept. 8 to Nov. 14, 2025.</p><p><b>City under siege</b>: The Blitz at times felt like a siege. The deportation campaign was one that residents could see, hear and feel. Helicopters hovered overhead for hours. Unmarked SUVs — sometimes without license plates — patrolled the streets, full of agents in military-style clothes. Neighbors' whistles and family members' screams became an unwanted daily soundtrack.</p><p><b>Total people detained</b>: During the height of the fall enforcement campaign, 3,841 people were detained in total. Nearly all were immigrants, held inside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in suburban Broadview, built to process immigrants over a few hours, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydvjujl-l-h/" target="_blank" >not to house people for days</a>. Detainees <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydvjujl-l-k/" target="_blank" >reported crowded, unsanitary conditions</a> behind doors <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydvjujl-l-u/" target="_blank" >closed even to clergy and members of Congress</a>. Federal officers detained children estimated to be as young as two and senior citizens as old as 76.</p><p><b>Background check</b>: The Trump administration vowed repeatedly that it was going after "the worst of the worst" criminals in the U.S. without legal status. Yet as federal officers detained record numbers of immigrants in Chicago-area detention facilities, the <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydvjujl-l-o/" target="_blank" >percentage of detainees with a prior criminal conviction fell to 15% from a high of 50% in January 2025</a>.</p><p><b>Total people deported</b>: The number of immigrants detained during the 10-week campaign who were later removed from the U.S. — either involuntarily or because they agreed to self-deport — reached a high during the blitz: 2,732.</p><p><a class="Link" south to Mexico.</p><p>Children and adults learned about the butterflies' migration patterns, enjoyed arts and crafts, took in cultural performances and watched monarchs be released into the sky.</p><p>Organizers said the event was meant not only to educate visitors about the science of monarchs, but also about the cultural significance of the species. Monarchs span much of North America during their migration and are symbols of resilience. In Mexican culture, they are also associated with Día de los Muertos, where their arrival is sometimes viewed as representing a spiritual connection between the living and the departed.</p><p>At the Judy Istock Butterfly Haven inside the museum, a father on Saturday comforted his nervous daughter as butterflies fluttered around a room that has been transformed into a lush forest.</p><p>"These butterflies aren’t dangerous," he explained. entries.title: Bears WR Rome Odunze "day-to-day" with injury; Ben Johnson 'hopeful' he'll play in season opener vs. Panthers
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> wide receiver <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/07/you-either-do-or-you-dont-bears-wr-rome-odunze-harsh-critic-of-himself-despite-improvement" >Rome Odunze</a> remains out with an apparent foot injury and won't practice Tuesday as the Bears prepare for their season opener Sunday against the Panthers. Coach Ben Johnson said he was "hopeful he'll be ready to go" for the game.</p><p>Odunze has been a concern since suffering a stress fracture in his foot last season and missing five games, but Johnson said this issue isn't related to that.</p><p>The Bears will practice Tuesday afternoon, then give players Wednesday off. Since Wednesday is the first day the team is required to release an injury report, the team will estimate players' availability.</p><p>Odunze likely would've been the Bears' leading receiver last season if he hadn't gotten hurt. Johnson referred to him at one point as quarterback Caleb Williams' "blankie" because Williams is so reliant on Odunze when under pressure.</p><p>Through the first 12 games last season, Odunze led the Bears with 44 catches for 661 yards and six touchdowns. He returned for the playoffs, but managed just four catches for 88 yards in two games.</p><p>He said in training camp his foot wasn’t affecting him, and the coaching staff seemed to agree that he looked as fast and agile as he did before the injury. He hadn’t missed any practice time until exiting the final preseason practice Thursday.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Bears name 5 captains for 2026 season
entries.summary: <p>Four of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' five captains will be doing it for the second-straight year.</p><p>A player vote selected five permanent captains for the 2026 season: quarterback Caleb Williams, guard Joe Thuney, defensive tackle Grady Jarrett, linebacker T.J. Edwards and kicker Cairo Santos. Bears coach Ben Johnson named the captains before Tuesday's padded practice at Halas Hall. The Bears will open their season on Sunday at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/07/bears-panthers-trade-2023-ryan-poles-caleb-williams-bryce-young-luther-burden-dj-moore-general-manager-nfl" target="_blank" >Panthers</a> at Bank of America Stadium.</p><p>"Huge recognition for those guys voted by their peers — and a lot of responsibility comes with that," Johnson said. "Obviously, they represent the locker room to the coaches but also to the fan base as well. They're everything we want to be about and they go about their business the right way. So, really proud of those guys."</p><p>Williams, Thuney, Jarrett and Santos were four of the Bears' five permanent captains last year, alongside safety Kevin Byard, who left in March to join the Patriots via free agency. The Bears had a whopping eight captains under coach Matt Eberflus in 2024, including Williams, who was then a rookie No. 1 overall pick, and Edwards. </p><p>On the Bears' roster, Santos, Jarrett and Thuney trail only third-string quarterback Case Keenum in terms of experience. <br></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Soccer spotlight to be on Chicago when Robert Lewandowski and the Fire host Lionel Messi's Inter Miami
entries.summary: <p>No offense to Caleb Williams, but the two most internationally famous athletes to play this year at Soldier Field will face each other Wednesday night in a soccer game.</p><p>Lionel Messi and Inter Miami are visiting Robert Lewandowski and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire" >Fire</a> at what’s expected to be a packed stadium. Both Messi and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2026/06/28/report-fire-set-to-sign-polish-superstar-robert-lewandowski" >Lewandowski are truly global icons</a> with legions of fans around the world, and their supporters will be watching the Fire and Miami in a match between two of the best teams in Major League Soccer.</p><p>The latter is what the Fire (11-6-5, 38 points) are trying to focus on. They enter the match in third place in the Eastern Conference, five points behind second-place Inter Miami (12-4-7, 43 points) but with a game in hand.</p><p>“The excitement and all the hype about the game is there. It's there for a reason,” Fire attacker Philip Zinckernagel said Monday. “But once the ref blows the first whistle, you're so into the game, it's just a game like any other game.”</p><p>Yes, technically, Zinckernagel is right that Wednesday is just another match during a grueling MLS season. It would be a surprise if he said anything else, and go against the expected ethos of professional athletes concentrating on what’s in front of their eyes.</p><p>Of course, there’s much more to it when figures like Messi and Lewandowski will share an MLS field for the first time.</p><p>Messi is the consensus greatest soccer player of all time. He collected trophies in Spain with Barcelona and a World Cup title with the Argentina national team to cement his legacy as the heir to Pele and Diego Maradona. His 2023 arrival instantly turned Inter Miami into the marquee MLS franchise and a traveling road show, with fans clamoring to see the aging but still excellent star.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-credit"><p>Keito Newman/AP Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Then there’s Lewandowski, who has six goals in eight league games with the Fire. Though his resume lacks Messi’s World Cup medal and success in the international game, Lewandowski accomplished everything else a soccer player can during a glittering European career in Germany and Spain. He’s also the greatest Polish player ever, making him an attractive drawing card in Chicago and elsewhere.</p><p>It’s coach Gregg Berhalter’s job to figure out how to restrain Messi and make sure the Fire are focused on the game and not the 60,000 fans at Soldier Field or the people who will tune in from all over the world to watch. At least Berhalter knows his players won’t need much motivation to show up Wednesday.</p><p>“It's pretty easy because these are the games that, if you're a player, you can't wait to play in. These are the games that you mark your calendar in the beginning of the year, that you're so excited for,” Berhalter said. “So, then it's about locking in. The adrenaline is going, and these are the games that are really easy to get up for.”</p><p>Since David Beckham joined the Galaxy in 2007, MLS teams have raced to sign their own international superstars. The Fire have done decently in that race, succeeding with Mexico’s Cuauhtémoc Blanco and German star Bastian Schweinsteiger.</p><p>Lewandowski is a bigger star than either of those players and he’ll be wearing Fire colors on the same field as Messi. Zinckernagel doesn’t expect the Fire to be distracted, noting that they’ve played in front of big crowds and hosted Messi before.</p><p>“I'm just happy that we have one of the superstars on our team this time,” Zinckernagel said. “It’s exciting, exciting times with the club and you want to play those games with a full stadium. Those are the fun games.”</p>

entries.title: Second racist Lincoln-Way East incident alleged by Homewood-Flossmoor
entries.summary: <p>On Tuesday, Homewood-Flossmoor revealed that a second racist incident occurred between the schools over the weekend. Several H-F athletes and coaches returned to campus after a girls cross country meet on Saturday and detailed the incident.</p><p>H-F released the following statement:</p><p>“Our athletes gave written statements that described what occurred while they were in the HF box before the start of the Varsity race on Saturday. Three HF athletes shared a description of one of the LWE coaches making comments about running 'past those monkeys' to the LWE team in the starting box directly adjacent. The athletes then reported that some of the team began cheering and making 'noises that were racist' and 'monkey gestures.' Upon their return and receiving the written statements, we notified LWE leadership.</p><p>Yesterday evening, our leaders followed up with LWE on what had been done and it was reported that the coach in question stated she was sharing with the LWE runners that they call that event the 'Jungle' and the HF team must have misunderstood what was said.”</p><p>Homewood-Flossmoor says it plans to pursue legal action on this second occurrence as well as the incident at the football game on Friday.</p><p>Lincoln-Way East principal Toriano Griggs addressed a possible student walkout in an email sent to school families on Tuesday. The walkout is a reaction to an incident of racial harassment that five Lincoln-Way East students committed during the varsity high school football game on Friday at Homewood-Flossmoor.</p><p>“We are also aware of information circulating about a potential student walkout on Wednesday, September 9,” Griggs wrote in the email. “While we will not prevent students from participating in a walkout, we will manage any student walkout or protest in accordance with procedures outlined in the student handbook and with appropriate safety precautions in place. Individuals who are not Lincoln-Way East students or authorized visitors will not be permitted on campus. Our priority will continue to be maintaining a safe and orderly environment for all students and staff.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racial-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >Lincoln-Way East students plan walkout over racial harassment incident at Homewood-Flossmoor football game</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/05/lincoln-way-east-homewood-flossmoor-racial-harassment" >Lincoln-Way East students accused of racial harassment at Homewood-Flossmoor football game</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Police removed multiple people from the Lincoln-Way East student section in the third quarter of Friday’s game between visiting Lincoln-Way East and Homewood-Flossmoor in Flossmoor.</p><p>Most fans and media were unaware of what happened, but photos and videos began appearing on social media Saturday morning. Later on Saturday, both schools addressed the incident.</p><p>According to a statement from H-F superintendent Jennifer Norrell and principal Clinton Alexander, “five Lincoln-Way East student fans made a very bad choice to engage in disrespectful and racist harassment towards H-F students seated in the bleachers.”</p><p>Alexander was at the game. The statement goes on to say that H-F is working with Lincoln-Way East and local authorities “as we consider all options to protect against this in the future, including legal options.”</p><p>Griggs addressed the incident on Tuesday in Frankfort with the Lincoln-Way East student body.</p><p>“By now, many of you have seen videos, social media posts, or news reports about the incident,” Griggs wrote in the email to families. “I have personally reviewed videos and spoken with students, families, and others who were there.</p><p>“I want to be very clear: the racial slurs, monkey noises, and racist gestures that occurred Friday night were hurtful and completely unacceptable. This behavior has no place at Lincoln-Way East or anywhere else.</p><p>“We reminded students that being a Griffin is about much more than wearing blue and white. It is about how we treat others, having the courage to speak up when something is wrong, and understanding the responsibility that comes with representing our school...Friday night was deeply disappointing. What matters now is how we respond, what we learn, and what we do moving forward. Our actions must demonstrate the values we expect from the Lincoln-Way East community.”</p>

entries.title: Adolescente embarazada es baleada en La Villita en día festivo
entries.summary: <p>Un muchacho de 17 años le disparó a una adolescente de 16 años embarazada durante una discusión en el vecindario de La Villita la noche del lunes, Día del Trabajo, informó la Policía de Chicago.</p><p>El presunto tirador, que ella conocía, y la adolescente discutían en la cuadra 2200 al sur de Sawyer Avenue cuando él abrió fuego y le disparó dos veces en la espalda antes de huir alrededor de las 7:10 p. m., según un reporte de policía.</p><p>La adolescente fue llevada al Hospital Mount Sinai y, según la policía, inicialmente fue reportada en estado grave.</p><p>La policía tiene un video del tiroteo grabado con un teléfono celular, según el informe.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-940000" name="module-940000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>No se han reportado arrestos.</p><p>Detectives de la zona investigan.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Winless Simeon stays optimistic due to talented sophomores Jalonny Billingsley and Aki King
entries.summary: <p>Simeon <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/05/morris-football-marion-persich-simeon" >lost at Morris on Saturday</a> to open the season 0-3. Such a challenging start could send many teams into an emotional free fall. But that isn’t the case with the Wolverines.</p><p>“I told the guys going into the season that we were putting them through a gauntlet,” Simeon coach Sinque Turner said. “After losing to East St. Louis last year in the playoffs, I didn’t think we were fully prepared based on the teams we had played during the season.”</p><p>So Turner went out and amped up his nonconference schedule. The Wolverines were competitive against Morris and Marist and lost to Bolingbrook by 31 points.</p><p>“We played well against all those teams,” Turner said. “If we eliminate some penalties and some self-inflicted wounds, those scores change a lot. But I’m not worried. We should win the next five games. Morgan Park will be waiting for us, and King is getting better, but they are not the same caliber as the three teams we just played.”</p><p>One of Turner’s major reasons for optimism is the talented young quarterback/receiver combo of Aki King and Jalonny Billingsley. The sophomores connected for touchdowns of 78, 55 and 34 yards against Morris.</p><p>King threw for 370 yards with no interceptions, and Billingsley had six catches for 194 yards.</p><div He has the potential to mature into one of the best receivers in the country over the next few years. King is fast and savvy; he also contributed 73 rushing yards.</p><p>The duo has been playing together since they were 12 years old as part of the Chicago Hellcats youth football program, which practices at Simeon.</p><p>“The future is bright,” Turner said. “We are definitely going to keep these guys together, and there will be more talented guys that want to come and join them.”</p><p>Billingsley, who is 6-4 and 180 pounds, is the cousin of former Phillips star Jahleel Billingsley, who went on to play for Alabama and Texas.</p><p>The cousins have never met, but Jalonny reached out to Jahleel a few years ago.</p><p>“We’ve been communicating,” Jalonny said. “He’s talked to me about football and told me to keep my game up. I’m looking forward to meeting him in person.”</p><p>Simeon’s King-Billingsley connection may be the Public League’s most dynamic force. And it is unlikely there is a more productive sophomore duo in the state.</p><p>“It is pretty special,” King said. “We know what we can do with the chemistry we have built together. Now we need to go out and make it happen.”</p><h3>Other slow starts</h3><p>There are a handful of prominent programs 0-3. Barrington, which opened the season at No. 16 in the preseason rankings, has suffered some key injuries and is winless.</p><p>St. Laurence and Lockport are both 0-3. The Vikings made deep playoff runs the last several seasons, and Lockport advanced to the Class 8A semifinals last year.</p><p>Warren and Prairie Ridge have been staples of the Super 25 for most of the past decade, and both teams are 0-3.</p><p>This is the best year in state football history to get off to a slow start, however. All three-win and many two-win teams are likely to qualify for the IHSA’s expanded playoffs. So every team in the state still has everything to play for.</p>

entries.title: Lakers will unveil Phil Jackson statue next year
entries.summary: <p>The Los Angeles Lakers will unveil a statue of former coach Phil Jackson outside their downtown arena next year.</p><p>The Lakers announced the plan Tuesday to honor Jackson, who led the Lakers to five championships and seven NBA Finals appearances during two stints totaling 11 seasons as their head coach.</p><p>The statue will be unveiled April 9 before the Lakers' home game against Minnesota.</p><p>After his famed tenure leading Michael Jordan's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> to six championships, Jackson joined the Lakers in 1999 and immediately began another era of major success for the 17-time NBA champion franchise.</p><p>His first three teams in Los Angeles won championships behind the dynamic duo of Kobe Bryant and Shaquille O'Neal, and the Lakers added two more titles in 2009 and 2010 led by Bryant and Pau Gasol. His Lakers also made the NBA Finals in 2004 and 2008.</p><p>Jackson set the Lakers franchise record for coaches with 610 victories while leading his teams to the playoffs in every year of his tenure, which ended in 2011.</p><p>"Phil Jackson defines championship basketball for a reason," Lakers governor Jeanie Buss said in a statement. "His masterful approach to coaching brought out the best in some of the greatest athletes to ever play the game. After he accepted my dad's invitation to join the Lakers, Phil's unmatched creativity and commitment to excellence restored our championship legacy, bringing five titles and setting a standard of excellence for generations to come. It is a great joy to be able to mark that achievement with the statue he so richly deserves."</p><p>Jackson will be the ninth person associated with the Lakers to be honored with a statue in Star Plaza outside their arena. He joins Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Jerry West, Elgin Baylor, Bryant, O'Neal, broadcaster Chick Hearn and former coach Pat Riley, whose statue was unveiled earlier this year.</p><p>Jackson's 11 championships as a head coach are the most in NBA history. The North Dakota native and former New York Knicks forward is a member of the Basketball Hall of Fame.<br></p>
