entries.title: Legislative watchdog Mike McCuskey resigning in wake of complaints over handling of Benton harassment case
entries.summary: <p>Illinois’ top legislative watchdog is resigning in the wake of complaints over his handling of sexual harassment investigations that have roiled Springfield, including accusations from one complainant that the former judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/31/harry-benton-report-legislative-inspector-general-speaker-chris-welch-sexual-harassment" target="_blank" ><u>didn’t take notes</u></a> or record their interview.</p><p>Legislative Inspector General Michael McCuskey will step down later this month while the bipartisan Legislative Ethics Commission that oversees the office seeks his replacement, officials announced Tuesday.</p><p>The commission said it received “notification of an upcoming vacancy” in the LIG position Aug. 31, as calls grew for McCuskey’s ouster in the weeks following the release of his report on disgraced former Plainfield state Rep. Harry Benton’s conduct.</p><p>McCuskey’s report concluded Benton broke state law by sexually harassing three women, including a lobbyist who later rebutted several “inaccuracies” in the inspector general’s report.</p><p>In an email, McCuskey said he tendered his resignation effective Sept. 30, “so I can complete the work of the office by the end of the month.” He declined further comment.</p><p>In a response from the lobbyist released along with the Benton report July 31, she disputed several points from McCuskey, who “did not record our one-on-one interview or take contemporaneous notes,” she wrote.</p><p>The lobbyist said McCuskey misreported the sequence of events after Benton made lewd comments, and she disputed a separate claim that McCuskey deemed unfounded: a complaint that Benton had photos on his phone of women in “various stages of undress which he claimed to be involved with romantically.”</p><p>“Every woman member of the General Assembly I interviewed said they had heard about the pictures on Benton’s cell phone, but could not identify anyone who saw the pictures,” McCuskey wrote. The lobbyist said she told McCuskey that Benton showed her such photos as well.</p><p>McCuskey, a former state and federal judge, stood by his report “completely.”</p><p>“I have never tried cases in the press. Nor will I ever do so!” McCuskey wrote in a July 31 response.</p><p>But he defended his handling of the case <a class="Link" href="https://www.theillinoize.com/articles/mccuskey-addresses-benton-welch-ammons" target="_blank" ><u>during a radio interview</u></a> last month, telling WMAY that he likes “to look the victim in the eye to get the feeling of anger, to get the feeling of being distraught... I don’t want my head down writing, which to me is [saying], ‘He’s just taking notes.’”</p><p>Arlington Heights state Rep. Mary Beth Canty, who chairs the House Democratic Women's Caucus, had called for McCuskey to step down or be removed after the lobbyist further claimed the LIG “violated the confidence of other victims and me, broke standard investigative norms, and made inappropriate comments,” according to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/08/28/lobbyist-illinois-inspector-general/?utm_campaign=mrf-twitter-chicagotribune&utm_source=twitter&utm_medium=social&mrfcid=202608296a8ed54199199a12cddb47c5" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Tribune</u></a> report.</p><p>In a statement Tuesday, Canty said “McCuskey’s resignation is significant, but it does not end the culture of harassment that has persisted in Springfield for far too long.</p><p>“We must strengthen the laws that guard against harassment, build a process that survivors can trust, and show the leadership required to earn the public's confidence,” Canty said.</p><p>The scandal has raised <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/19/chris-welch-state-fair-illinois-house-sexual-harassment-harry-benton" target="_blank" ><u>uncomfortable questions</u></a> for Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch, who was aware of a separate complaint against Benton about two years earlier but still directed $1.4 million into Benton’s 2024 reelection campaign.</p><p>And it has all underscored a perpetual culture of harassment in Springfield less than a decade after the #MeToo movement spurred lawmakers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/11/5/18375535/state-lawmakers-appoint-inspector-general-amid-harassment-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>to fill a two-year vacancy</u></a> in the legislative inspector general’s office. McCuskey, 78, has held the post since 2022.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has urged lawmakers to bolster Springfield’s process for handling sexual harassment allegations.</p><p>“Obviously, [McCuskey] made a mistake in the way he talked about this,” Pritzker said. ”I can't speak to whether or not he should step down… I do think that the entire matter that came before him and the legislative committee that considers breaches is one that needs to be thought about an awful lot over the next month or two.”</p><p>McCuskey faced more questions for his swift dismissal of allegations from a former staffer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/20/amy-briel-laura-jackson-chris-welch-lig-investigation-harassment" target="_blank" ><u>against state Rep. Amy “Murri” Briel, D-Ottawa</u></a>.</p><p>McCuskey told the Sun-Times he deemed Laura Jackson’s complaint unfounded, but she told <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/09/04/michael-mccuskey-legislative-inspector-general-sexual-harassment-victims-rich-miller" >Capitol Fax</a> the explanation she got was that “I was an at-will employee and that there wasn’t really anything that they could do for me… I was never told that anything was unfounded or anything like that.”</p><p>House Minority Leader Tony McCombie, R-Savanna, called McCuskey’s resignation “an opportunity to strengthen the office of the LIG, to fix the culture of harassment apparent within the House majority, and update Illinois’ ethics laws.”</p><p>“The legislature should move quickly to strengthen anti-corruption safeguards and increase the jurisdiction and authority of the office of the LIG,” McCombie said in a statement. “House Republicans have legislation ready that should be taken up during the veto session.”</p><p>State Rep. Jeff Keicher, the Sycamore Republican who chairs the Ethics Commission, said they were committed to filling McCuskey's position "in a timely manner.” They're seeking applications through Oct. 31.</p>

entries.title: Local elected officials, residents decry plan to move Sox out of Bridgeport — and Amtrak in
entries.summary: <p>More than a hundred people gathered outside the White Sox’s Rate Field Tuesday to decry a plan that would move the team from Bridgeport to the South Loop, and in turn put an Amtrak maintenance facility in their neighborhood.</p><p>White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia's company, Canal Edge LLC, has proposed a mixed-use development called The Railyards as the site for a new stadium, which would be built where an Amtrak railyard now operates — and across the Chicago River from the Chicago Fire's stadium at the 78. </p><p>The ballpark itself would be privately financed, a source with direct knowledge of the planning told the Sun-Times. But there would be an ask for public funding for local infrastructure, including for nearby roads, bridges and potentially a new Metra station, although those details are far from finalized.</p><p>Ald. Nicole Lee (11th), whose ward includes Bridgeport, said 35-year-old Rate Field has "life left" in it — though the area around it needs sprucing up. Lee’s office said Ishbia hasn’t reached out to her office to discuss how his plan would affect local residents.</p><p>“Taken together, this plan would be devastating for our community,” said Lee, who live just hundreds of feet from the proposed site of the new Amtrak facility. “We know we have to modernize the stadium, and modernize and develop these areas along 35th Street. We stand ready to have those conversations. … No 24-hour maintenance facility belongs in a residential area.”</p><p>Amtrak has said more than $600 million in federal funds is earmarked for building a new maintenance facility at the current site of a Union Pacific railyard in Bridgeport, near Rate Field. That project is also being partly financed by Ishbia's company.</p><p>Amtrak received a federal “<a class="Link" href="https://www.doi.gov/oepc/nepa/categorical-exclusions" target="_blank" >categorical exclusion</a>” for the project, which is expected to start this fall. That allows it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances."</p><p>In recent months, a coalition has formed around addressing the environmental and economic impact a Sox stadium move and expanded Amtrak presence would have on the neighborhood.</p><p>So far, Amtrak’s attempts at dialogue with residents has been limited to setting up two community meetings, Lee's staff added, one of which was postponed after the alderperson's office told Amtrak to come to the next one more prepared to answer residents' concerns.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >New Sox Park? Future owner Justin Ishbia announces proposal for riverside stadium at ‘The Railyards’</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" >Who is Justin Ishbia, the White Sox’ potential future majority owner?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><p></p><p>U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, a North Side Democrat who is running for mayor, serves on the House appropriations committee and the subcommittee on transportation. He conceded Amtrak needed a new maintenance facility but opposed Canal Edge's proposal — and threatened federal funding for the company.</p><p>“If they ever want help from me, or the appropriators of the delegation again, they won’t stand against you all,” Quigley said. “They need to know they can’t use preemptive powers to force this over a community’s will.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c70000" name="image-c70000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bcd3fe4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fc5%2F2ebbe36248eb9779edf3dca27fb0%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-07.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/53a4083/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fc5%2F2ebbe36248eb9779edf3dca27fb0%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-07.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c5dad61/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb5%2Fc5%2F2ebbe36248eb9779edf3dca27fb0%2Fsoxstadiumfolo-260909-07.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="U.S. Rep. entries.title: Michigan falls out of AP Top 25 as LSU moves into the top 10
entries.summary: <p>LSU jumped back into the top 10 in the first Associated Press Top 25 college football poll of the regular season on Tuesday, Oregon slipped out of the top five and Michigan fell out of the rankings altogether after it needed a second-chance Hail Mary try at home to beat Western Michigan.</p><p>Ohio State remained No. 1 by a wide margin entering its showdown with No. 4 Texas on Saturday. The Buckeyes received 46 first-place votes from the voting panel of 69 writers and broadcasters. The other 23 first-place votes were divided among six teams.</p><p>Georgia, Notre Dame, Texas and Indiana each moved up one spot with Oregon going from No. 2 to No. 6 following a 34-27 win over Boise State as a 25.5-point favorite. Miami, LSU, Mississippi and Texas A&M rounded out the top 10.</p><p>Defending national champion Indiana received the second-most No. 1 votes, with eight. LSU got five, Notre Dame four, Oregon three, Texas two and Miami one.</p><p>LSU made one of the biggest statements of Week 1 with its 51-10 rout of Clemson in Lane Kiffin's debut in Baton Rouge. Courtroom drama over the eligibility status of LSU players trying to return to college from NFL training camps took the spotlight in the days leading up to the game, and then Sam Leavitt and his highly paid teammates made fast work of Clemson.</p><p>LSU's rise from No. 11 to No. 8 gave the Tigers their first top-10 ranking since they were No. 4 after a 4-0 start last season. The Tigers went 3-6 the rest of the way, Brian Kelly was fired at midseason and Kiffin was hired away from Mississippi with the charge of restoring LSU to its former glory.</p><p>LSU's promotion bumped Oklahoma out of the top 10. The Sooners shut out UTEP 51-0 and will take a No. 11 ranking into their visit to Michigan. That matchup lost some luster in light of Michigan's slogging offensive performance against Western Michigan, a game the Wolverines won 13-12 after one second was put back on the clock at the end of the game. That was just enough time for Bryce Underwood to throw a second Hail Mary, this one landing in the hands of JJ Buchanan.</p><h3>In and out</h3><h3></h3><p>Virginia rode an impressive Week 0 win over North Carolina State to a No. 25 ranking. It's the first time since 2005 the Cavaliers have been ranked in a first regular-season poll. They finished No. 16 in the final Top 25 last season but received just one vote in the preseason poll.</p><p>Michigan went from No. 16 to to out of the Top 25, the first time since at least 2008 that a team ranked so high was bounced after a win. Kansas State went from No. 17 to unranked after holding off North Dakota of the Football Championship Subdivision last year.</p><h3>Poll points</h3><h3></h3><p>• Seven teams with first-place votes are the most since the same number got first-place votes in the 2016 preseason poll. It's the most in a regular-season poll since seven got first-place votes Sept. 2, 2014.</p><p>• Of the 25 ranked teams, 24 won in the same week for the first time since Week 1 in 2019.</p><p>• Louisville held onto its No. 24 ranking after losing 41-38 to Mississippi on a walk-off field goal. entries.title: Lonnie Bunch III, Chicago historian named secretary of Smithsonian, to step down at end of year
entries.summary: <p>Lonnie Bunch III, who led the charge to build the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture and formerly served as the Chicago History Museum president, will step down from his post as the 14th secretary of the Smithsonian, he said in a statement Tuesday.</p><p>A historian by training, Bunch became the first Black person and first historian appointed to the position atop the Smithsonian — the world’s largest museum — in June 2019. His efforts to <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/09/03/arts/design/smithsonian-bunch-trump.html" target="_blank" ><u>maintain the museum’s independence</u></a> amid an internal review initiated by President Donald Trump’s administration <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/08/letter-to-the-smithsonian-internal-review-of-smithsonian-exhibitions-and-materials/" target="_blank" ><u>“to assess tone, historical framing, and alignment with American ideals”</u></a> put him at odds with the president. </p><p>Bunch said in the statement Tuesday that he leaves the Smithsonian with “pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” He plans to step down at the end of the year, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/08/arts/design/smithsonian-secretary-lonnie-bunch-resigns.html" target="_blank" >The New York Times reported.</a></p><p>The secretary of the Smithsonian is responsible for 21 museums and 14 research centers.</p><p>Bunch, who ran the Chicago Historical Society (later renamed Chicago History Museum) from 2001 to 2005, was the driving force behind the creation of the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History. The $540 million project, which began during the administration of George W. Bush, opened in 2016 during the tenure of President Barack Obama.</p><p>Bunch told the Chicago Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/9/24/18379342/sweet-chicago-treasures-at-new-african-american-museum" target="_blank" ><u>in 2016</u></a> that his political dealings in Chicago — including with former Mayor Richard M. Daley, former Gov. George Ryan, the leaders of the Illinois General Assembly and Chicago’s corporate community — taught him “the power of a marriage that includes the corporate community, the political community and the cultural community.”</p><p>The D.C. museum featured many Chicago artifacts, including a Pullman porter cap, a pew from the Quinn Chapel AME Church and furniture from the set of Oprah Winfrey’s show.</p><p>Bunch<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2019/10/15/in-new-memoir-smithsonian-secretary-lonnie-bunch-iii-finds-hope-in-history" target="_blank" ><u> told WBEZ’s Reset</u></a> in October 2019 that he wanted to steward a project that told many viewpoints.</p><p>“One of the things that was so important was to realize there wasn't a single African American experience,” he said. “So we really tell stories through the lens of Chicago or Birmingham so that people get a sense that this is an amazingly complicated community. But maybe the most important thing we do is all of those stories are done in a way that said this is not a separate story about the Black experience. It is really using the African American experience as a lens to understand what it means to be an American.”</p><p>Museums, he told Reset, should not just be backward-looking.</p><p>“I really do think that if the museum is just about yesterday, then it fails,” he said. “But if it helps us think about yesterday, today and tomorrow, then it becomes a place that is valued and contributes in a way to making a country better.”</p><p>Last summer, the White House issued an executive order titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History” that initiated a review of the Smithsonian’s public-facing content, exhibition materials and curation process. The initial review focused on eight museums, including the National Museum of African American History and Culture, the National Museum of American History and the National Portrait Gallery. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/08/letter-to-the-smithsonian-internal-review-of-smithsonian-exhibitions-and-materials/" target="_blank" ><u>The review</u></a>, the White House said, was intended to “ensure alignment with Trump’s directive to celebrate American exceptionalism, remove divisive or partisan narratives, and restore confidence in our shared cultural institutions.”</p><p>A subsequent 162-page report by the Domestic Policy Council, issued <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Smithsonian-Report-Saving-Americas-Story.pdf" target="_blank" ><u> in July,</u></a> criticized the National Museum of American History and its director for “failing” to illuminate the nation’s heritage and displaying materials “intended to undermine faith in American institutions.”</p><p>In a memo, <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/style/2026/07/08/full-text-lonnie-bunch-memo-smithsonian-white-house-report/" target="_blank" ><u>obtained by the Washington Post,</u></a> Bunch defended the institution: “At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America's story,” he wrote. “As public servants and the keepers of this institution, we are charged with helping a nation find understanding, hope and clarity and as part of that duty, we are dedicated to excellence, reflection and growth."</p><p>Bunch told The New York Times it was not the pressure that had led to his resignation.</p><p>“It was really just saying, now’s the time.<i>”</i><br></p>

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson plays security guard in Mannings' video
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson was one of 40 people who made a cameo appearance in a 16-minute long video promoting another season of ESPN’s popular “ManningCast.”</p><p>In the "Oceans 11"-style short film, Peyton and Eli Manning try to infiltrate the NFL’s offices to find the schedule for their show. Johnson plays a security guard inside the offices — as do Jim and John Harbaugh of the Chargers and Giants, respectively; Titans coach Robert Saleh; Rams coach Sean McVay; Texans coach DeMeco Ryans; Chiefs coach Andy Reid; and former Dolphins coach Mike McDaniel.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/08/bears-name-captains-ben-johnson-caleb-williams-joe-thuney-grady-jarrett-cairo-santos-tj-edwards-nfl" target="_blank" >Johnson</a> had two lines, which he spoke into a walkie-talkie with commissioner Roger Goodell on the other line.</p><p>“I think I just saw them,” Johnson said. “It’s the Mannings.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">2 Brothers, 40 Cameos, 0 Clue. <br><br>Peyton & Eli take matters into their own hands to adjust the ManningCast schedule. <a href="https://x.com/OmahaProd?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@omahaprod</a> <a href="https://t.co/FLpL0Lbmfw">pic.twitter.com/FLpL0Lbmfw</a></p>— ESPN (@espn) <a href="https://x.com/espn/status/2097301427706044652?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 8, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Celebrities from outside the NFL world who appeared in the video include Larry David, Anne Hathaway, Paul Rudd, Jon Hamm and Glen Powell.</p><p>The "ManningCast" will air alongside the Bears' Nov. 2 "Monday Night Football" game in Seattle.</p>

entries.title: Death of CTA passenger shoved off moving Red Line train at 69th Street probed as homicide
entries.summary: <p>Detectives are looking for three attackers after a CTA passenger was shoved off a moving Red Line train and landed on the electrified third rail Monday afternoon in the Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood, officials said. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/09/07/labor-day-weekend-shooting" target="_blank" >The death marked the ninth homicide of the long holiday weekend. </a> </p><p>About 2:30 p.m. Monday, a fight erupted aboard the train in the first block of West 69th Street, and three people involved in the altercation pushed a 29-year-old man off the train, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man, who came in contact with the third rail and possibly also hit by a train was dead on the scene, according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. A Tuesday autopsy was inconclusive and pending further studies. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/07/cfd-1-dead-on-cta-red-line-tracks-near-63rd-street" target="_blank" >Earlier, police said the victim had jumped from the train. </a></p><p>Area 1 detectives are conducting a homicide investigation. No arrests have been reported. <br> </p>

entries.title: Rejecting cruelty of a nation bent on squashing trans Americans
entries.summary: <p>The war on trans Americans continues unabated. The government cashiers loyal and effective soldiers from the military while trying to quash health care for young people nationwide. Apparently, parents know what's best for their own children only when denying them vaccines. A scary time, and if you don't think it's your problem, then you're ignoring how quickly a cruel and arbitrary government can shift from one target to another. Hate is fickle.</p><p>Civility shouldn't be. I've been defending trans people in print for 34 years. First, because I'm a Jew, and given our history of being on the receiving end of hatred, it's our responsibility not to limit the compass of our sympathy entirely to ourselves.</p><p>But there's another reason, one I've never explained, So today I'll tell the story.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-170000" name="module-170000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>As a young reporter, I quickly discovered there are two ways to do the job. You can wait for someone to assign you something, and end up covering fires and zoning board hearings.</p><p>Or you can find your own subjects, ones that you are guaranteed to be interested in because you picked them yourself.</p><p>I preferred the second path.</p><p>So I'm combing the classified ads at the back of the Chicago Reader, fishing for leads, when I notice an ad for a boutique on Elston Avenue selling women's clothing in large sizes to men.</p><p>"Now <i>there's </i> an interesting business," I thought, and headed over. Talking to the owner, I realized this is more than one shop. This is a world, a community. I saw an announcement for a dance, and decided to go.</p><p>At the dance I met "Jenny," who I described in the opening paragraphs of my story this way:</p><p><i>"Jenny has sparkling blue eyes, a small, upturned nose and a cascade of curly blond hair tumbling over her right shoulder.</i></p><p><i>"With a rhinestone nail charm centered on each red fingernail, a dab of blush at her decolletage, and deftly applied make-up, it's easy to believe her when she says she spent three hours getting ready to go out.</i></p><p><i>"The shimmery blue and silver dress is custom-made, she says, and it's easy to believe that, too, since with the spike heels, Jenny tops out at perhaps 6-foot-7.</i></p><p><i>"'I'm a bigger girl, I know,' she says, smiling radiantly. 'I can't go out to a mall — hey, I've got a football player's shoulders.'"</i></p><p>What I did not put in the story was my thought processes, standing there in the dim, loud dance, with my narrow pad and pen, as she spoke. Picture me, brow furrowed, gears slowly turning, as I looked up at this young woman, nearly a foot taller than myself.</p><p>"Hmmmm...." I thought. "Three hours. That's a long time. She must really want to do this. You know ... most people do what they really want to do. And in that sense, I'm lucky that what I really want to do is go home and kiss the wife. Because if I wanted to do ... what she wants to do ... I'd be completely screwed. Because I could either do what I want to do, and be this loathed pariah skulking around the shadows. Or I could spend my life not doing what I want to do, and isn't that a sad way to live?"</p><p>Remember, this was in 1992. That society would become more accepting, for a while, was beyond my imagination. And don't put too much importance on "want to do" as opposed to "have to do." I can't gauge the impetus driving someone to change such a fundamental aspect. But it must be powerful. In the face of enormous societal pressures — grief from your family, and now the government going after you — people make the leap anyway.</p><p>That moment of sympathy stayed with me, and tells me the current furor over trans people is all wrong, because it's driven by demagogues, jabbing a stick into the most controversial aspects — restrooms and athletics. Those are not important, but rather harms being posited. Haters are cowards. They gin up these theoretical hurts and wave them over their heads, trying to justify themselves. I'm not saying toilets and swim meets aren't concerns. I'm saying that for them to be Topic No. 1 is like arguing in 1930s Germany about whether Jews exert undue influence on banks. It's buying the slur and missing the point.</p><p>The key question is: when a person decides to live a life authentic to who they are, how is that person to be received? With kindness or hostility? With acceptance or rejection? Myself, I can't imagine putting stumbling blocks in front of such a person. It seems needless cruelty.</p><p>But there's a lot of cruelty going around. Another key question is: are you opposing this cruelty? Or adding to it?</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg
